terrain.difficultyNotes: A three-tier breakdown, so percentExpert is null and the top 29% sits in percentAdvanced. Everything in this group comes from OnTheSnow rather than the resort: attitash.com is entirely JavaScript-rendered and its mountain information page returns no readable statistics to either the fetch tool or curl with the project's bot user-agent, which is the same problem Stratton presented in Batch 2. Attitash is really two mountains - Attitash proper and Bear Peak, linked mid-mountain - and the 73-trail count covers both. Note the 88-inch snowfall figure, the lowest of any mountain in this guide: the Mount Washington Valley floor sits at 600 feet and gets a great deal of what falls as rain.

passes.name: Epic Local Pass
passes.access: Unlimited - Attitash is on the Epic Local unlimited list alongside Crotched Mountain, Mount Snow, Mount Sunapee, Okemo and Wildcat

pricing.notes: 2026-27 season. Vail prices day tickets dynamically by date and publishes no fixed window rate, so the ticket fields are null rather than estimated. The season pass figure is the full adult (31+) Epic Pass; Vail does not sell an unrestricted Attitash-only pass. Attitash carries unlimited access on the cheaper Epic Local Pass too, at $829 for 31+, which is the tier most New England Epic buyers actually want. epicpass.com and attitash.com were both returning errors on the verified date, so the figures come from OnTheSnow's Epic buyer's guide; that guide quotes $1,089 in its prose, which was the March 2026 on-sale price, while its current cost line reads $1,119.

editorial.overview: Attitash is the mountain the Mount Washington Valley actually skis, and it is a more interesting place than its statistics suggest. Seventeen hundred and fifty feet of vertical across two linked peaks - Attitash proper and Bear Peak - on 311 acres in Bartlett, ten minutes from North Conway and all the lodging, food and outlet shopping the valley has. That location is the whole proposition: Attitash is where a family staying in North Conway goes, and it is priced into the Epic Pass at the unlimited tier on both the full pass and the Local, which makes it close to free for anyone who already has one. The skiing is honest intermediate terrain with a long runout, a three-mile top-to-bottom, and a top 29% that is respectable rather than fearsome. The problem is elevation. The base sits at 600 feet, the summit at 2,350, and 88 inches of average snowfall is the lowest total in this guide by a wide margin - what falls on Wildcat as snow arrives here as rain more often than anyone would like. Attitash lives or dies on its snowmaking and on the calendar. In a cold February it is a genuinely good mountain. In a mild one it is the thinnest big-name mountain in New Hampshire.
editorial.snowQuality: The weak point, and the numbers are blunt about it. Eighty-eight inches a year is the lowest average of any resort in this guide - a third of what Jay Peak claims and less than half Wildcat's, twenty minutes up the road but two thousand feet higher. The reason is elevation: a 600-foot base in the Mount Washington Valley floor catches a great deal of rain in storms that fall as snow on the surrounding mountains, and the lower third of the hill takes the worst of every thaw. Snowmaking covers 240 of the 311 acres, and it is doing the heavy lifting all season rather than just at the margins. This is a mountain to ski in a cold spell, and one where checking the base-area report matters more than at almost anywhere else.
editorial.crowds: Busier than it looks on paper, because Attitash draws from a large lodging base rather than from day-trippers. North Conway fills up over school holidays and February vacation, and the valley's visitors distribute themselves between Attitash, Cranmore and Wildcat - with Attitash taking the largest share of the families. Eight lifts across two linked peaks spreads people reasonably well, and Bear Peak stays quieter than the Attitash side. The pattern worth knowing is that Epic Pass access at the unlimited tier makes this a default choice for a lot of New England passholders, so weekends draw a passholder crowd on top of the resort's own guests.
editorial.difficulty: Comfortable rather than testing. The three-tier split puts 49% in the middle grade and 29% at the top, which is an accurate description - this is a mountain of long, well-cut intermediate trails with a three-mile top-to-bottom run and enough pitch on the upper sections to keep a competent skier interested. The two-peak layout adds variety that the acreage does not suggest, and there is glade skiing. What is missing is anything sustained or steep enough to worry an expert, and the low-elevation base means the bottom third is often the least pleasant part of the run rather than the payoff. Anyone in the valley looking for real difficulty drives to Wildcat.

keyTrails.name: The Mountaineer
keyTrails.note: The summit lift, and the one that defines a day here - it serves the top of Attitash proper and the longest sustained descents on the hill.

keyTrails.name: Bear Peak
keyTrails.note: The second mountain, linked mid-mountain and consistently quieter than the Attitash side. Worth crossing over for on a busy holiday week.

keyTrails.name: Flying Bear
keyTrails.note: The lift that opens up the Bear Peak terrain. Where regulars go when the main side fills up.

keyTrails.name: Abenaki
keyTrails.note: One of the quads on the Attitash side, serving the middle-mountain intermediate terrain that is the bulk of what people ski here.

tidbits: Attitash is two linked mountains - Attitash proper and Bear Peak - counted as one resort.
At 88 inches, Attitash has the lowest average snowfall of any resort in this guide.
The 600-foot base elevation is the lowest of any mountain in this guide.
Attitash is unlimited on the Epic Local Pass as well as the full Epic Pass.
It is ten minutes from North Conway, which gives it a lodging base most New Hampshire areas lack.

moguls.policy: No grooming policy could be sourced. Attitash's own site publishes nothing readable and no independent review consulted discusses its grooming or names a bump run, so what is recorded here is limited to what the terrain and snow conditions imply rather than anything stated.
moguls.quality: Genuinely not documented, and this file says so rather than filling the gap. What can be said from the sourced figures is structural: an 88-inch average snowfall and a 600-foot base mean Attitash depends on machine snow for most of its surface, and a heavily snowmade surface gets groomed to stay usable. That points to a mountain where bumps form between passes on the steeper upper pitches rather than one with maintained mogul terrain, and the presence rating reflects that inference. Anyone in the Mount Washington Valley specifically wanting bumps should drive to Wildcat, which does not groom its blacks at all.

parks.overview: Nothing citable. Attitash's own site is JavaScript-rendered and returns no readable park information, OnTheSnow publishes no park count for it, and no independent review consulted covers the parks. User reviews on OnTheSnow mention a small terrain park, which is a hint rather than a source. This is the thinnest parks section on the roster and it should be revisited once the resort's site is readable.
parks.reputation: No sourced assessment exists. The one recurring remark in user reviews is that the park is small, which is consistent with a Vail-run valley mountain whose identity is family intermediate skiing, but it is not enough to write a judgement on.
